meta.headline: Reality check (2026-06-20): an earlier conclusion said Keepance was 'finished and just needs marketing.' Recent hands-on Windows testing proved that wrong — there are many unfinished and broken areas. The honest picture: a lot is built, but the product is NOT finished. Getting it genuinely reliable (especially on real Windows and Mac) is active, necessary work — alongside, not instead of, solving distribution.
meta.updateRule: High bar: a Claude session only updates this for a MAJOR decision, a validated insight, a strategy shift, or a real milestone. Routine work never touches it. Jameson maintains it freely.

sections.title: Strategy & Vision
sections.now: Keepance is sharpened from a general 'private AI workspace' into one clear identity: the private intelligence layer for a law practice — a desktop app where a lawyer's documents, email, and matters live on their own machine, stay private by design, and answer questions back with citations they can click and verify. The lead audience is deliberately narrow: solo and small-firm litigation lawyers first. The positioning is set and a lot is built — but recent Windows testing shows the software itself is not actually finished.
decisions: Repositioned to law-first (2026-06-09): one audience, one job — 'find anything across a matter with a citation you can click.'
Lead niche locked as litigation solo/small-firm (tax and consulting kept as backup angles).
Earlier sequencing (2026-06-17): 'finish the vision, then go sell.' This is now in question — see the correction below.
insights: CORRECTION (2026-06-20): the 2026-06-17 conclusion that the product is 'mature/finished, so the only job is distribution, not building' was overturned by real Windows testing. Substantial unfinished work remains, so finishing and hardening the product is back on the critical path — alongside distribution, not after it.
Open board question: is the priority now (a) finish the product to genuinely reliable, (b) hand-sell to lawyers, or (c) both in parallel? This is a real decision to make, not a settled one.

Honest tension to protect: 'nothing leaves your machine' is fully true only in the slower local-AI mode; the recommended higher-quality mode sends data to the lawyer's own AI provider. The product frames this honestly as a privacy spectrum.
Open question: set a 'kill-criterion' — a fixed window of effort with an honest agreement on what 'it's working' vs 'pivot' looks like.

sections.title: Marketing
sections.now: There is a large, well-organized marketing library — channel playbooks, email sequences, press kit, comparison pages, battlecards — but almost none of it is currently driving traffic. The website drew ~225 visitors over a recent ten-week stretch, nearly all typing the address in directly, meaning search, social, and referrals send almost nobody. Channels were re-pointed (2026-05-27) toward where lawyers actually look.
decisions: Channel pivot (2026-05-27): primary channels are now legal-industry outlets (ABA TECHSHOW, Lawyerist, Above the Law, IPWatchdog), not Product Hunt / Hacker News.
'Marketing-led only' model (2026-06-06): assumes no personal network and no warm intros — every tactic must work cold.
All public copy bound to a strict voice guide (first-person, plain, no AI-cliché words, no em dashes, every claim linked).
insights: The website's convert-the-visitor page is strong, so the failure is upstream — almost nobody arrives. A distribution problem.
Credibility play: own an empty lane — 'private by architecture, not by promise.' No analyst currently champions local-first legal AI.
Near-term move: pitch the leading legal-tech journalist (Bob Ambrogi / LawSites) and apply to a conference startup showcase (ABA TECHSHOW Startup Alley).
Caveat (2026-06-20): don't market hard until the product is genuinely reliable on the platforms users run — shipping traffic to an unfinished app burns the first impression.

sections.title: Sales
sections.now: There is no sales motion yet and no paying customers. The agreed plan is founder-led hand-selling, not self-serve signups or ads: pick one type of lawyer, run live 10–20 minute demos on the prospect's own real case file, and sell the outcome. Pricing, demo content, and objection scripts are prepared; what's missing is the selling activity itself, which is Jameson's to drive.
decisions: Sell by hand, not by funnel (2026-06-17): hand-sell the first ~10 customers one at a time.
Recruit 3–5 'design-partner' lawyers on free pilots, to convert into named testimonials.
Win solo lawyers first, not firms: the firm tier needs trust credentials Keepance doesn't have yet.
Demo weighting: ~70% on the outcome (does the work, won't waive privilege or leak client data), ~30% on the privacy architecture.
insights: Four objections mapped for every demo: AI quality, IT setup burden, 'a DIY box is less secure,' and 'no security certification yet.'
The strongest real pain signal in the whole record came from a financial advisor (Jameson's wife), NOT a litigator — so the chosen audience has technically never been validated. A genuine risk.
Checkout snag for real sales: buy buttons still route through a shared store branded 'projelli,' so a lawyer sees an unrelated brand at checkout. Needs its own branded store before any real sale.
Caveat (2026-06-20): a live demo on real Windows will expose the unfinished areas — finish the demo path before showing it to a lawyer.

sections.title: Growth & Traction
sections.now: The honest weak point. By every measurable signal, Keepance is at idea-validation stage commercially. Verified directly from the systems (not estimated): zero real paying customers, zero genuine license activations (only Jameson's own tests), an empty firm-accounts database, ~225 website visitors in ten weeks (almost all direct), ~17 downloads of the latest version, a handful of 'buy' clicks ever, and empty email signup lists. And the product underneath is feature-rich but not yet finished.
decisions: Name the reality plainly: a feature-rich but unfinished product meeting an untested market — both finishing it and reaching buyers are real work.
Define an explicit success/failure test (the kill-criterion) so effort has an honest checkpoint.

UPDATED (2026-06-20): the earlier 'stop treating a sales problem as a build problem' framing is corrected — real Windows testing shows there genuinely IS unfinished build work; it's not avoidance to finish it.
insights: The math is encouraging IF reach is solved: customers bring their own AI key, so cost per customer is near zero — even a modest number becomes real income.
Binding constraints, in order: (1) a genuinely finished/reliable product, (2) reach/distribution, (3) demo-to-close, (4) retention. Price is NOT the constraint.
A 'lifestyle business' income is reachable at a fairly small customer count; a 'real company' would need the firm tier or a repeatable channel.
Structural risk: one non-developer operator, no sales experience yet, and a product that still needs a real finishing pass.

sections.title: Competitive & Market
sections.now: Keepance occupies a genuinely unique spot: the only tool across legal, tax, consulting, and advisor AI offering a true local / nothing-leaves-your-machine option (competitor sweep, 2026-06-08). Incumbents (Clio Duo, Thomson Reuters CoCounsel, Microsoft Copilot, LexisNexis) are all cloud-based; the closest local rival (Elephas) is Mac-only with no legal features. But the market's default answer is 'cloud with strong assurances,' and lawyers are mostly moving toward the cloud, not away.
decisions: Keep a running competitor-watch log — the one event that most threatens Keepance is an incumbent adding a local or zero-egress option.
Frame the pitch as 'the most provably-private way to get AI's benefits,' NOT 'the cloud is unsafe' — the absolutist framing alienates the ~75% of lawyers already cloud-comfortable.
Keep competitor-comparison pages reconciled to current facts.
insights: Encroachment to watch: LexisNexis 'Protégé' (Feb–May 2026) added customer-held encryption keys for big firms. Honest counter: it still routes data through their cloud; only a local model removes the trip entirely.
Well-funded rivals are mostly in adjacent categories (Jump $80M, Zocks $45M for advisors; Blue J $300M+ for tax) — they prove the space is hot but don't attack the local-first wedge.

Two citable legal angles: a Florida Bar opinion (local AI removes client-consent paperwork) and a 2026 federal ruling, U.S. v. Heppner (consumer-AI chats aren't privileged). Heppner is real — never delete it.
Counter-pressure: 'bring your own key' is no longer unique, and a self-hosted box with no certification can be harder to defend than hardened cloud — a real objection.

sections.title: Engineering
sections.now: Keepance has a lot built — version 3.x, signed installers for Windows/Mac/Linux, and a deep feature set (Word editing with AI tracked-changes, ask-across-your-files-with-citations, email import/search, single sign-on, an encrypted vault, live co-editing). But recent hands-on testing on real Windows hardware (2026-06-20) revealed many unfinished and broken areas. The honest status: feature-rich but NOT finished or production-solid. Earlier notes calling it 'mature and shipped' were too optimistic — see the Testing tab for where it actually stands per platform.
decisions: Redirect effort toward making the product genuinely reliable (not net-new features) — and now, explicitly, toward finishing the broken/unfinished areas Windows testing exposed.

Fixed several self-contradictions and customer-safety issues (2026-06-17): a removed feature still shown to paying customers; a paid tier advertising credentials that don't exist; silent file-save/audit-log failure paths.
Latest fixes are written and tested but NOT yet released — cutting a new signed build is a slow, costly step that waits for Jameson's explicit go-ahead.
insights: CORRECTION (2026-06-20): 'the product is mature, more features won't move the needle, stop building' is wrong. Real Windows testing found many unfinished items beyond the logged bugs — the product needs a genuine finishing pass.
New capability: Claude can now drive the real desktop app on a Windows test machine like a user — far faster/cheaper bug-finding than the old hour-plus build-and-check loop.

Known logged bugs (a partial list): privacy indicators disagreeing on the active AI provider; email connecting but never syncing; a stuck sync that shows no error (BUG-008). Jameson found more during recent testing — to be detailed in the Testing tab.
Connectors to outside legal systems (Clio, iManage, Office add-ins) are blocked on vendor access — outside Keepance's control, deliberately deferred.

sections.title: UX
sections.now: The app is reshaped around the law-practice identity with a clean, navy-railed layout organized by what a lawyer does (Matters, Search, Documents, Email, Workflows, Activity Log, Settings). A long polish pass (2026-06-16) tightened onboarding and settings. A standout theme is making privacy visible: an always-on indicator of where data is going, a 'Where your data is' map, and a printable Confidentiality Report. Real Windows use shows there are still rough and unfinished flows to fix.
decisions: Trust as a visible product surface (2026-06-17): turned the privacy story into things a prospect can see and screenshot.
Hallucination guardrails in the experience: uncited answers carry a 'verify before relying on this' warning, and a one-click 'verify against source' flags fabricated citations.
Honest onboarding: recommends the higher-quality bring-your-own-key mode as default, and presents max-privacy local mode honestly as 'more private, less capable for legal work.'
insights: Defensibility hinges on never quietly being wrong — a confidently-wrong answer is a malpractice/sanctions risk, so citation + verification is core.
The email feature is the daily-use beachhead ('find anything in your mail, with a citation, even when Outlook search fails') — but it's one of the areas recent testing showed is not finished.
Real-world UX papercuts logged (a failed search clears your typed question; a stuck email sync gives no feedback) — and likely more from recent Windows testing.
Open idea: an opt-in, off-by-default 'design-partner' mode that learns from real usage without breaking the no-spying promise (structure only, never content).

sections.title: UI
sections.now: There's a real two-layer design system (built 2026-06-15): shared style tokens (color, spacing, type, shadows) plus a library of reusable building blocks (buttons, toggles, search fields, cards, badges). It covers the whole app, so the same control looks and behaves identically everywhere. The theme is a polished light look (light background, dark text, navy accent). Some real-hardware visual checks remain.
decisions: Adopt the shared design system everywhere; stop using one-off hand-styled elements so the UI can't drift.
A fixed layout law for every screen: header, then one tools row (buttons → toggles → filters → search), then content.
Rebrand cleanup: replaced leftover 'projelli' branding with the correct Keepance shield identity — confirmed on real Windows.
insights: Because Keepance sells trust, visual consistency is itself a trust signal — a sloppy interface reads to a lawyer as an unreliable product.
The design-system push was triggered by concrete inconsistencies (two differently-sized 'New' buttons; clashing filters).
Genuinely Windows/Mac-only visual checks (real Word interop, native folder picker, the auto-updater) still want real-hardware spot-checks — tracked in the Testing tab.

sections.title: Testing
sections.now: Tracks how thoroughly Keepance actually works on each operating system its customers use. Headline: automated checks are strong on Linux (our build machine), but recent hands-on Windows testing exposed many unfinished and broken areas, and Mac is largely untested on real hardware. This is a primary focus, not a solved problem. (Jameson is filling in the specific findings.)

platforms.detail: The build/dev machine. Thousands of automated checks run here — unit, integration, browser, and a real-desktop harness — giving good coverage. But Linux is not a typical customer platform, so green here does NOT mean green for real users.

Recent hands-on testing on real Windows hardware (2026-06-20) exposed numerous unfinished and broken areas — this is the platform most customers use and the priority to finish. Some specific bugs are logged and fixed-in-source (email connectors, AI chat reachability, a stuck sync with no error message); Jameson found many more during testing, to be listed here as he goes.
Not yet validated on real Mac hardware. A borrowed Apple machine is planned as a test bench. Treat Mac as unverified until a real-hardware pass happens.

sections.title: Jameson's Questions
sections.now: Big questions where I (Jameson) use AI to help me think them through and understand them. Each has a short overview here and links to a full research write-up.

questions.q: Do our target users use Mac or Windows more?
questions.answer: Windows, by a wide margin. The ABA's solo/small-firm survey puts ~81% of these lawyers on Windows vs ~11% on Mac — and among solos specifically (our core user) Mac is highest at ~16%, about 1 in 6. Mac rose into 2021 but has been flat/volatile since, so there's no rising-Mac trend to bet on. Takeaway: polish Windows first (~4 of 5 users), support Mac well as a strong second (small but vocal, influential community), keep Linux a low-priority long tail — which matches our Testing priorities. Caveat: we have no first-party data yet (our traffic is too low and mostly us); worth turning on OS tracking.

questions.q: What else could I be doing with AI to push this project forward?
questions.answer: A lot — and the highest-leverage moves aren't 'write more code.' Top 3: (1) have AI test the real Windows app like a lawyer every day and report breakages in plain English with screenshots; (2) build one fake litigation case file to use as both the testing yardstick and the sales demo; (3) run an AI 'lead-finding engine' that surfaces 25–50 specific litigation lawyers a week with tailored outreach you just approve. Also: an AI sales copilot (call briefs, follow-ups, objection cards), a weekly legal-tech radar, and in-product features aimed at litigation pain (contradiction finder, privilege-log draft, citation verify). Skip the low-value stuff: daily social spam, generic SEO blogs, big autonomous agents.

sections.title: Finance & Metrics
sections.now: There is no real revenue and no live customer metrics — the honest state. The old financial plan (one-time price, a target with no customer-cost math) was retired; a new model was built (2026-06-17) around the real pricing. Pricing is per-seat ANNUAL: Solo $468 / Professional $948 / Firm $1,548 per seat (min 3 seats). A founding cohort gets 30% off for life; pre-3.0 one-time buyers are grandfathered forever.
decisions: Move to per-seat annual subscriptions in three tiers (2026-06-09) — well below specialized legal AI, at-or-above generic productivity AI.
Protect the local-first soul with a 'your files are always yours' guarantee — cancelling turns off AI features and updates, never your data.
Treat acquisition cost as time-bound, not cash-bound: spend is ~$0; the real cost is founder hours.
insights: The one durable bright spot: customers bring and pay for their own AI key, so cost per customer is near zero — roughly 95% gross margin. The only number in the model that isn't an assumption.
Rough scenario framing (assumptions, not forecasts): first ~10 customers ≈ $5–9K/yr; a comfortable lifestyle level ≈ $60–90K/yr; a 'real company' ($250K+) needs the firm tier or a repeatable channel.
The firm tier can't scale on 'trust me' — company-scale revenue depends on a trust moat (formed entity, a data-processing agreement, a SOC 2 certification, named references) that doesn't exist yet.
Re-run the whole model with real numbers only after the first ~10 customers; until then, don't steer by it.
